statement: Excel under the hood, modern on the surface: the calculation engine and file format stay Excel so every workbook opens and calculates in Excel, while the front end presents multiple views over the same model without ever altering calculation.
why: Lets humans and AI agents build Excel-compatible models and present them far more attractively than a raw grid without sacrificing Excel compatibility.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Layer 1 (Engine and document) comprises calc-host, calc-doc, and the Excel model; front-end views must never reach directly into them.
why: Enforces clean separation between calculation semantics and presentation skins.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Layer 2 (the view contract / Skin IR) exposes four pillars: neutral targets (cells, ranges, names, tables, objects, layout items), one command vocabulary (Excel commands plus view layout commands), projections built from neutral data, and subscriptions ('viewing is subscribing').
why: Gives every view and custom skin one uniform, grid-agnostic protocol over the workbook.

statement: A view may perform only operations a user could perform in Excel, plus arranging its own view layout.
why: Preserves the 'no more than Excel' calculation invariant across all views.

statement: Layer 3 is one shared shell surrounding every view, providing files, recent/templates, print and page setup, add-ins, settings, search, command palette, undo history, and macro security identically in the browser and on the desktop.
why: Avoids duplicating chrome and keeps workbook-level workflows consistent across all views and platforms.

statement: Layer 4 consists of five persona-driven built-in views plus any skin authored by a user or AI agent.
why: Separates persona workflows into tailored views while keeping extensibility first-class.

statement: Classic view (for Excel users, finance, operations) provides a grid, formula bar, sheet tabs, and tabbed command bar with Excel's structure under DNA Calc's own visual design (no Microsoft icons, fonts, or styling), backed by an explicit keyboard and mouse gesture conformance list (Alt key tips, Ctrl/Shift navigation, F2/F4/F9, Ctrl+Enter, fill handle and double-click fill, drag-move, formula range-picking).
why: Preserves Excel muscle memory for power users while respecting visual IP boundaries.

statement: Inspector view (diagnostic, after Phyphox; for reviewers, auditors, developers, debugging agents) is read-mostly and systematically exposes precedents/dependents, calc chain and order, evaluation traces, volatile/dirty state, names, errors and their origins, add-in and RTD activity, timings, and file parts.
why: Turns opaque spreadsheet calculation internals into systematic diagnostic instruments.

statement: Notebook view (for analysts, educators, write-ups) presents a Jupyter-style chain of input cells (each formula visible as written) with each result directly beneath and the next input building on it, with prose between and live Pluto/Excel recalculation (not run-once), treating dynamic arrays/Tables as data frames with inline charts/shapes, live RTD, sheet-control panels, vertical or horizontal cross-sheet pipeline layouts, and an optional live-tree extension.
why: Combines narrative analytical flow with Excel's always-live dependency recalculation.

statement: Model map view (for modellers, engineers, systems thinkers) renders names and blocks as boxes, references as wires, hierarchical blocks (sheet, table, or group opened to its inside), state and feedback (z^-1, iteration), and optional sheet pages.
why: Makes system architecture, hierarchy, and feedback loops directly visible.

statement: App view (proposed fifth view, for people who use a model without building it) presents the model as an author-laid-out application—input form, results, charts, and scenario controls—with all underlying spreadsheet mechanics hidden.
why: Replaces brittle Excel workarounds built with locked sheets and buttons.

statement: Thin formula rewriting (presenter/interpreter) is an optional lens any view can enable to display formulas in a more readable form (names, LET, lambda structure) with strictly identical calculation meaning.
why: Improves formula legibility across views without changing workbook semantics.

statement: FRONT_END_SCOPE originally proposed storing view layout and metadata in CustomXML (`urn:dnacalc:view-manifest`) with hidden defined names as anchors, relying on Excel ignoring and preserving them on save (round-trip to be proven in dc-1nbp.22). (Note: hidden-name anchors are later overridden by DECISIONS_20261126 ruling 13.)
why: Keeps presentation metadata inside standard Excel files without breaking Excel.

statement: A workbook may declare a preferred view and a set of supported views; every view must still open every workbook correctly, though an undesigned view may appear plain.
why: Guarantees no workbook is ever locked out of any view while letting authors guide first presentation.

statement: Views can be mixed per sheet within one workbook—for example, a notebook sheet feeding a grid sheet with a model-map sheet over both.
why: Matches real workbooks whose tabs serve distinct roles (data, computation, narrative, overview).

statement: VBA and add-ins preserve Excel's object model, and Classic view exposes the missing UI members: Selection, ActiveCell, ActiveWindow, and the status bar.
why: Maintains compatibility with existing VBA macros and add-ins that inspect or drive Classic UI state.

statement: Non-Classic views get a small DNA Calc views COM library so macros can switch views, select a block, or show a panel, designed once the views settle.
why: Allows automation to interact cleanly with modern views without distorting Excel's core object model.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Skins are declarative manifests naming theme tokens, layout regions, keymap, commands, and panels; imperative code is used only to introduce new components.
why: Makes safe skin authoring and restyling accessible to users and AI agents.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: A published skin SDK ships four parts—the view contract, component library, manifest schema, and an automated harness that loads any workbook, screenshots each view, and runs the keyboard/gesture conformance list—enabling an agent to edit, verify, and ship a skin.
why: Closes the loop for autonomous agentic UI customisation with objective visual and interaction verification.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Safety guarantee: a skin cannot alter calculation because it holds no engine handle—only the view contract whose commands are Excel's—upholding 'no more than Excel'.
why: Makes user and agent front-end customisation structurally safe by construction.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: 2026-11-20 baseline built status: a two-tier contract exists (host-side HostSession/SkinIntent; page-side Skin/Controller over a 70-intent wire protocol with tile batches and semantic RenderPlan), six experimental DNA Calc skins (grid DOM/Canvas2D, notebook, ledger, atlas, tree, canvas) route through it without reaching the engine, and the view manifest exists (written only by notebook).
why: Establishes the pre-cleanup starting baseline for skin architecture refactoring.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: 2026-11-20 architectural leaks identified: grid-shaped Controller, skins building raw intents while neutral Target went unused, per-skin projections and chart/wire SVG assembled in the worker (visual edits touched worker code), single active view only, and desktop shell decoding protocol messages.
why: Names the specific abstraction leaks blocking clean multi-view skins and agent customisation.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: 2026-11-20 unbuilt capabilities: formula presenter/interpreter, name-backed blocks and Model map, multi-view support, UI automation, declarative skin manifest/SDK, and Formula Explorer on the shared host contract.
why: Enumerates the major front-end capabilities missing at the time of the scope draft.

statement: FRONT_END_SCOPE proposed a milestone sequence: (1) design sweep producing contract v2, manifest schema, and clickable prototypes; (2) contract refactor (split Controller, page-side projections/SVG, adopt Target); (3) Classic gesture polish; (4) skin SDK & harness validated by agent restyle + App build; (5) Notebook v2, Model map, Inspector.
why: Sequences contract foundations before building out the full persona views and SDK.

statement: DNA OneCalc is renamed publicly to 'DNA Calc - Formula Explorer', built on a two-level host contract: level 0 (formula host: CalcFml, CalcFunc, formatting, conditional formatting, add-in UDFs, no calc-engine) and level 1 (workbook host built on level 0).
why: Preserves honest engine-free layering for formula evaluation while unifying OneCalc and DNA Calc on one contract.

statement: Skin 0 (Formula Explorer) is a tool on level 0 only—not a workbook view on par with the five views—appearing both inside DNA Calc (opened from shell or cell 'explore this formula' with a snapshot of precedent values) and standalone as 'DNA Calc - Formula Explorer' without a workbook; the honest-layering rule checks level 0's dependencies (with calc-host placement open to decide).
why: Gives users one formula-exploration tool in both embedded and standalone contexts without duplicating code or leaking engine dependencies.

statement: The front-end implementation plan takes the Pro 19 synthesis's R-list (front-end requirements) and C-list (plain system needs) as its requirements, maps each C item onto underlying crates/layers without redesigning the UI, and keeps implementation detail out of the UX design brief.
why: Maintains a crisp separation between UX specification and internal Rust/protocol architecture.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Implementation ground rules: the engine does no more than Excel; page code never reaches engine or document code (enforced and extended by build checks); every step keeps the six current skins working (note: later superseded for post-book fresh UI rewrite by DECISIONS_20261126 ruling 10); no behaviour is lost without an explicit bead; development runs on Linux in checked batches.
why: Protects architectural layering and prevents regressions during refactoring.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: 2026-11-22 code baseline — Contract & Controller: HostSession/SkinIntent (calc-host) and Skin/Controller (dna-calc) communicate over 70 intents, 74 requests, 50 replies, 7 events, 4 FromServer envelopes, TileBatch, and RenderPlan; dc-xfrhg.3 split controller.rs (5,578 -> 3,181 lines / 2,263 prod) into a view-neutral core plus clipboard, editing, files, and grid.rs (1,145 lines), tested so non-grid skins never import GridController or crate::grid.
why: Documents the exact post-cleanup contract and controller boundaries for architecture planning.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: 2026-11-22 code baseline — Typed commands & worker: dc-xfrhg.2 eliminated raw protocol Intent construction in production skin code (82 -> 0) via 67 WorkbookCommand operations over dna_calc_model::Target plus 14 shell Commands (non-intent Requests remain); dc-xfrhg.5 unified six worker cell-assembly paths into Workbook::wire_cell/wire::cell_of/cells::value_or_refused (byte-identical across 12 replies), while per-skin projections and chart/canvas SVG drawing remain worker-side.
why: Records what is already clean versus what still must move to the page side.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: 2026-11-22 code baseline — Views, shell, Formula Explorer, manifest, VBA, FerroUI: Model::active_skin holds only one active skin with no ViewId; desktop shell app.rs is decoupled from wire decoding (3 -> 0 decoders via shared message.rs, keeping OpenNative/add-in intercepts); Classic grid parity stands at 8 Done / 23 Partial in UI_REVIEW.md; Formula Explorer still has its own port/Link/shell and RTD admission remains in calc-host/src/recalc.rs; calc-doc manifest v1 codec supports 4 skins while only notebook writes placements and Excel round-trip (dc-1nbp.22) is unproven; calc-vba is the sole live VBA reader (0 disagreements across 4,426 files); FerroUI 0.5.0 Linux prototype exists (dc-etcxb.2).
why: Gives skin-architecture designers verified file-level facts rather than stale assumptions.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Work area 1 (Contract v2): adopt Target everywhere with a typed command layer mapping every action to an Excel operation, add ViewId and multiple subscriptions, and separate view state from workbook state.
why: Enables concurrent multi-view and per-sheet mixed views over one workbook model.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Work area 2 (Controller split, done in dc-xfrhg.3): keep a small view-neutral controller core (session, commands, subscriptions, undo) separated from the grid module so all non-grid skins depend only on the core.
why: Prevents grid assumptions from leaking into Notebook, Inspector, Model map, and App skins.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Work area 3 (Page-side projections): the worker sends only neutral data (values, formulas, regions, dependency summaries, chart series) so skins assemble their own projections and render their own SVG on the page side.
why: Decouples visual iteration and custom skins from worker/Rust backend changes.

statement: Work area 4 (Decoupled shell): the shell issues commands only—never decoding protocol internals—and one shared shell serves both browser and desktop, retiring OneCalc's separate shell.
why: Eliminates duplicate shell maintenance and enforces the command boundary.

statement: Work area 5 (Inner-layer C-list queries and events): provide region/name-level dependency queries, calc chain and order, region/pattern detection (sheet-as-database, input blocks, time series, etc.), scoped change events, incremental paged projections, and level-of-detail summaries for large sheets—each with an explicit latency and memory budget.
why: Supplies the engine-neutral data queries required by Inspector, Notebook, Model map, and Enron-scale workbooks without hangs.

statement: Work area 6 (Persistence): implement one unified view-manifest reader and writer in calc-doc for all views with per-sheet view choice and preferred/supported views, anchor references (brief notes defined names; see DECISIONS_20261126 D-13 override), reconciliation after edits made in Excel, and a proven Excel round trip.
why: Ensures view layouts survive real-world Excel editing and saving.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Work area 7 (Skin manifest and SDK): deliver the manifest schema and loader, theme tokens, keymaps, component library, and the boundary for extension code.
why: Provides the concrete authoring surface for declarative skins and safe coded extensions.

statement: Work area 8 (Test harness): automatically open corpus workbooks in every view verifying no crash/hang, latency/memory budgets met, and zero calculated values altered by any view; verify the Excel file round trip and Classic gesture conformance list; capture screenshots including a large-workbook tier drawn from Enron (20.7M formula cells).
why: Mechanically proves views never corrupt Excel answers and remain responsive at real corpus scale.

statement: Work area 9a (Level-0 formula host): encapsulates formula entry/evaluation, function catalogue/help, completion, value display, number formatting, conditional formatting, and add-in loading/UDF registration (.xll, COM, VBA); its dependency closure includes CalcFml, CalcFunc, calc-value, formatting kernels, add-in hosts, and calc-doc for its constrained file, and must never include calc-engine.
why: Guarantees Formula Explorer and formula-bar services share one engine-free implementation.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Work area 9b (calc-host boundary decision): the architecture plan must first decide between (a) hosting level 0 inside calc-host as an engine-free formula tier vs (b) placing level 0 beside or below calc-host so level-0 callers bypass calc-host—weighing mechanical enforcement (crate boundaries hold whereas cargo features unify across a workspace and erode), level-0 session state ownership (UDFs, RTD topics, options), session object count for skins, and moving RTD admission out of calc-host/src/recalc.rs.
why: Prevents accidental dependency creep from calc-engine into level-0 formula tooling.

statement: Work area 9c (Level-1 workbook host & skin level declaration): level 1 (cells, ranges, recalc, tiles, subscriptions) builds on and reuses level 0 without copying it; every skin declares the host level it needs, and DNA Calc's formula bar, help, and formatting call the same level-0 services.
why: Eliminates duplicate formula-UI logic between Formula Explorer and workbook views.

statement: Work area 9d (Formula Explorer dual deployment & retirement of OneCalc shell): Formula Explorer is a level-0 tool—inside DNA Calc it receives precedent values as a snapshot from level 1 (never reading the workbook) and commits edits via a level-1 command; standalone 'DNA Calc - Formula Explorer' strips DNA Calc to skin 0 and level 0 only; the sweep ceiling check moves to level-0 closure; OneCalc's separate port, Link messages, desktop dependency on dna-onecalc, and separate shell are deleted while internal OneCalc identifiers are kept.
why: Consolidates two separate apps into one layered build with enforced zero-engine weight.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Work area 10 (Cleanup): delete everything contract v2 replaces—dead intents, per-skin worker projections, duplicated message handling, and the retired second VBA project reader.
why: Prevents dead parallel paths from lingering after refactoring.

statement: Implementation plan deliverables: beads under one epic ordered by dependency in batches with test-named acceptance criteria, milestones (never calendar dates), per-step record of deletions/compatibility/proof tests, risks paired with the step that retires each, and minimal owner questions.
why: Ensures the architecture plan executes cleanly and verifiably across parallel lanes.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Owner direction (2026-11-20 #1a-b): audit the skin API, Skin IR, and OneCalc to ensure every front end routes through the abstraction, and treat the front end as a customisation interface for agents so users and agents can alter display and behaviour without touching the engine.
why: Makes agentic customisability a primary architectural goal rather than an afterthought.

statement: Owner direction (2026-11-20 #1c): rethink front-end modes around personas—diagnostic (Phyphox style), Excel-compatible ribbon and grid (within copyright limits), Jupyter+Pluto live notebook (data frames, inline charts/shapes, RTD, controls, horizontal/multi-sheet pipelines, live tree extension), hierarchical blocks-and-lines with optional sheet pages, plus one additional mode to discover (became App).
why: Aligns each view to a distinct real user task rather than arbitrary visual skins.

statement: Owner mantra: 'Super Excel-compatible in the engine, and modern in the presentation.' All views share one shell (files, printing), sit as skins over one engine with thin formula rewriting, store extra view detail in CustomXML with preferred/supported/mixed views, keep every file openable in Excel, and may expose a DNA Calc skin COM library for VBA.
why: Summarises the unifying product thesis behind all front-end decisions.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/SKIN_DISCUSSION.md ¶2 (L15); restated in Pro 21 §Why another round ¶1 (L15)

statement: Owner direction (#2): Classic is an Excel-familiar skin with DNA Calc's own visual design and a strong focus on keyboard and mouse gesture fidelity.
why: Confirms Classic prioritises interaction muscle memory over visual cloning.

statement: Owner direction (#3): non-grid views must simplify or decline large workbooks and busy sheets, be tested against corpus large workbooks, and ground their UX in real spreadsheet/systems patterns such as sheet-as-database.
why: Prevents views from collapsing on real enterprise workbooks.

statement: Owner direction (#4): preserve OneCalc's honest engine-free layering and usable function/formatting/CF/add-in testbench by making it skin 0 ('Formula Explorer' tool inside DNA Calc, and 'DNA Calc - Formula Explorer' as a stripped standalone build), keeping 'OneCalc' as the casual internal name (dc-sdzi1) and leaving calc-host's boundary to be decided.
why: Eliminates dual-app maintenance while keeping honest CalcFml-only layering.

statement: Owner direction (#5): UX design briefs must avoid internal implementation details ('inside baseball') and focus on design philosophy, detailed mockups, and fleshed-out user experience.
why: Prevents architectural constraints from distorting user-experience exploration.

statement: Owner direction (#6): circular references are not delays; use an RTD source as the tick generator for simulation models (dc-hul4), and verify all concerns in full-fidelity HTML mockups (Pro 20).
why: Maintains strict Excel semantic honesty while still supporting true time-stepped simulations.

statement: Owner direction (#7, #9 correction): the defining attribute of Jupyter is seeing the input formula cell and its result beneath it as a visible computation chain—the next input building on that result—rather than merely a presentation reading layout; presentation layouts are secondary views of that chain, and Pro 21 must flesh out the computation notebook plus fuller standalone Formula Explorer and remaining gaps.
why: Corrects earlier briefs that over-indexed on reading-order presentation and under-specified active computation.

statement: Owner direction (#8): defer design merging to Sunday morning to address four questions—how to merge without losing ideas, the ~100-page Design Book, a feature-by-feature review, and planning the skin architecture.
why: Sets the four-part scope for the front-end consolidation round.

statement: Owner direction (#10 on Pro 21): keep the computation chain, named outputs, and backing cells; simplify the Author layout and mode; clarify or reconsider whether Author and Read need to be separate modes (resolved in DECISIONS_20261126 D-6: no separate read-mode presentation).
why: Prevents unnecessary modal complexity in Notebook.

statement: Standing product rules: the engine does no more than Excel; views use only what Excel exposes; desktop uses WebView2 with a grid fast enough for WebGPU; macro security levels are Off / Guarded / Unguarded; plan by milestones, not calendar dates.
why: Records non-negotiable standing constraints shared across all front-end work.

statement: Front-end design consolidation (epic dc-etcxb) gathers all framing docs, briefs, and multi-model answers around five core deliverables/questions: (1) lossless merge method (MERGE_PROMPT_PROVISIONAL.md), (2) ~100-page DNA Calc Design Book specifying every skin requirement and the skinning API, (3) feature review comparing current apps vs design, (4) skin architecture implementation plan (FRONT_END_IMPLEMENTATION_BRIEF.md), and (5) FerroUI vs Leptos/WebView2 evaluation (dc-etcxb.1-.3).
why: Defines the structure and outputs of the front-end design epic.

statement: 2026-11-22 progress snapshot: skins internals cleaned up (dc-xfrhg: 82 -> 0 raw intents, controller 5,578 -> 3,054 core + grid adapter, desktop on command path, unified worker cell assembly); Classic grid parity expanded across point mode, F4, Enter/Tab walks, Ctrl+arrow, system clipboard/Paste Special, fill handle, status aggregates, context menu, sheet tabs, Find/Replace/Go To, panes, resize/AutoFit, hide/unhide, zoom, notes/hyperlinks, spill explanations, merge, CF manager, and DV keyboard; FerroUI Linux prototype done; 42-page local site preview built.
why: Captures concrete shipped front-end baseline entering the merge.

statement: Complete front-end design source corpus for the merge: framing docs (LEGACY_DESIGN_REFERENCES, FRONT_END_SCOPE, FRONT_END_IMPLEMENTATION_BRIEF, SKIN_DISCUSSION, ferroui-eval), briefs (Pro 19, 20, 21), answers (GPT-6 Pro 19 with 34 C-needs/68 R-reqs, Pro 20 43 scenes, Pro 21 73 scenes superseding Pro 20, Fable 5.2 Pro 19, Gemini 4 Carbon Pro 19 with 18 scenes, Gemini 4 Neon Pro 19 with R-1..R-48/C-1..C-32 and 17 scenes), and design context (STRAND, LINKED_BOXES_SKIN, names-in-motion/watershed previews, dc-hul4).
why: Establishes the exact closed set of sources that Stage 1 ledgers must cover completely.

statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: one workbook, one selection, one undo history; switching views changes only presentation.
why: Guarantees spatial and transactional continuity across all views.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L49)

statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: every edit made outside the grid must be explicitly labelled as either a model change or a presentation change before it commits.
why: Prevents silent confusion between spreadsheet mutations and view-only layout tweaks.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L50)

statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: the formula lens is strictly read-only; 'Rewrite as LET' is an explicit model edit shown as a preview before applying.
why: Ensures a display lens never silently mutates workbook formulas.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L51)

statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: a per-sheet view is a preference surfaced via a badge, never an unexpected automatic view switch.
why: Prevents disorienting context jumps while navigating tabs.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L52)

statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: the Model map is a reader first; wiring edits come later and operate only on named ports; boxes created on the map are real cells with names on a visible sheet.
why: Keeps map authoring grounded in inspectable, Excel-compatible workbook cells.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L53-L54)

statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: Inspector diagnostic tools are also available as panels inside every other view.
why: Lets users inspect provenance, errors, or live signals without losing their current view context.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L55)

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Four-answer Pro 19 consensus: skins embedded inside a workbook file are declarative manifests only; coded components must be installed, signed extensions.
why: Eliminates untrusted code execution inside workbook presentation metadata.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L56)

statement: Owner-accepted Pro 19 push-backs: (1) a circular reference is not a delay; (2) a dependency picture is not an execution recording; (3) the 'Excel keeps it' CustomXML claim must be tested against an explicit matrix of save routes; (4) keeping a file intact is not the same as being able to run it everywhere.
why: Locks in four core honesty guardrails across Model map, Inspector, and Persistence.
evidence: docs/design/front-end/README.md §What the four Pro 19 answers already agree on (L57-L61)

statement: Eight cross-answer disagreements catalogued for owner/decider resolution (subsequently ruled on in DECISIONS_20261126): standalone Formula Explorer timing, F9 vs RTD clock for Run/Step, snapshot undo across macro runs, Excel-visible mirror for notes/findings, Excel key-tip letter parity, Ctrl+Alt+1..5 view keys, hidden names as anchors (Fable opposed), and persisting the agent's change trail in the file.
why: Tracks the exact set of conflicts across Pro 19 answers requiring explicit rulings.

statement: Carried-forward legacy Strand reference: palette roles, contrast pairs, density, and geometry in docs/plan/STRAND.md, with the `dna-strand` crate defining the authoritative shipped tokens.
why: Anchors the new Design Book in the existing Strand token system.

statement: Carried-forward legacy Shell reference (SHELL_SPEC): shell anatomy and keyboard atlas specifying how shell chrome, command surfaces, and focus move together, adapted to current desktop and skin boundaries.
why: Preserves proven keyboard-first focus and command-surface navigation patterns.

statement: Carried-forward legacy Interaction Mechanisms reference (MECHANISMS): interaction traces covering navigation, previews, selection, and visible provenance used as review scenarios for the current design.
why: Provides concrete cross-view continuity and preview-seam interaction mechanics.

statement: Carried-forward legacy Parity and Trust UX reference (PARITY_TRUST_UX): defines evidence states and their granularity for verifying a cell, function, or workbook, grounded in CalcVerdict's provenance and captured Excel results.
why: Ensures UI trust and parity readouts reflect real oracle evidence rather than vague claims.

statement: Carried-forward legacy Flow reference (FLOW_DESIGN): first-use walkthrough and keyboard map for notebook-style exploration (while leaving behind the legacy host's old skin IR and build plan).
why: Supplies tested onboarding and keyboard ergonomics for notebook exploration.

statement: Carried-forward legacy OneCalc formula editor notes (FORMULA_EDITOR_AND_ARRAY_RESULTS, APP_UX_FORMULA_EDITOR_SPEC, WS14): native browser input model, caret measurements, and revision rules carried into the shared formula UI context.
why: Avoids re-learning browser IME/caret/revision pitfalls in the shared formula editor.

statement: Carried-forward legacy OneCalc large-array results notes (FORMULA_EDITOR_AND_ARRAY_RESULTS, WS14): bounded typed preview, visible truncation notices, and predictable copy semantics for large spilled arrays.
why: Prevents UI freezes on huge array outputs while keeping truncation honest.

statement: Carried-forward OxDoc format references: standards index, Foundation identifiers, and CalcDoc fixture disposition available locally in docs/FORMAT_REFERENCES.md.
why: Grounds CustomXML and OOXML persistence rules in verified format specifications.

statement: Carried-forward OxCalc grid performance register (CORE_ENGINE_GRID_PERF_REGISTER): seeded workloads and counts of visited cells, edges, and bytes provide comparable workload baselines alongside DNA Calc's single-evaluator corpus and benchmark commands.
why: Provides repeatable large-grid stress metrics for front-end and projection budgets.

statement: Carried-forward OxCalc W048 circular-reference Excel observation ledger: records Excel build (16.0.19929 Windows en-ZA), iteration settings, thread modes, and 12 core + 19 bit-exact probes; single-thread and multithread observations must be kept distinct when interpreting cycle behaviour.
why: Anchors circular-reference and iterative-calculation UX explanations in real Excel behaviour.

statement: Carried-forward OxFml W074 name and call resolution freeze: distinguishes call position from bare value use, sheet scope from workbook scope, and ordinary names from table context; built-ins win tested call collisions, visible defined names win non-built-in UDF collisions, and LET/LAMBDA locals plus scalar vs callable defined names follow the oracle precedence matrix.
why: Governs formula completion, formula lens rewriting, and defined-name box resolution honestly.

statement: Strand token authority: canonical design tokens live in `apps/dna-strand` (where the crate and `STRAND.md` disagree, the crate wins); apps currently use system UI and monospace font stacks because Recursive and Source Serif 4 are not yet bundled.
why: Prevents spec-to-code drift in visual tokens and clarifies current font shipping state.

statement: Strand temperament is flight-deck, not showroom: derived from the DNA Kode mark (rounded blocks in petrol, teal, and amber), dark calm chrome holds the instruments, work sits on bright paper, color appears only when it carries meaning, dense where the hands are and generous where the eyes rest.
why: Sets the overall aesthetic tone across every DNA Calc view and tool.

statement: Strand Tenet 1 (Cockpit chrome, daylight work): petrol chrome holds instruments while the model sits on paper so chrome never competes with data.
why: Keeps user attention on workbook values and structure rather than application chrome.

statement: Strand Tenet 2 (Everything is a block): the base-pair rounded rectangle is the atomic visual unit for cells, nodes, formula tokens, name chips, and map districts, sharing one radius scale and one gap scale.
why: Creates visual coherence across Classic, Notebook, Inspector, Model map, and Formula Explorer.

statement: Strand Tenet 3 (Color is a signal, not paint): amber is now/focus, teal is structure, green is a fresh value, signal orange is external/volatile, and red is error—and nothing else, ever.
why: Preserves immediate semantic scannability by reserving saturated hues strictly for state.

statement: Strand Tenet 4 (One material, many states): one variable typeface morphs sans<->mono so UI, values, and formulas share one skeleton, while Notebook prose uses a quiet serif.
why: Makes formulas feel native to the same material as values while distinguishing explanatory prose.

statement: Strand Tenet 5 (Modeless truth): one bit separates SELECTED from EDITING; ghost previews appear before commit, Esc is always an exact revert, and legality is shown before the user pays (preview seam).
why: Eliminates modal traps and makes edits predictable and reversible.

statement: Strand Tenet 6 (Instruments, not ornaments): provide persistent honest readouts and use motion only when it carries meaning (120-160 ms settle; recalc ripple along real evaluation order).
why: Avoids distracting animation while making real state transitions legible.

statement: Strand Tenet 7 (Every object has an address): node path, A1, defined name, and table column share one addressing grammar for goto, peek, and automation—what a human types is what an agent sends.
why: Unifies human navigation, inspection, and agent automation under one target grammar.

statement: Strand Tenet 8 (Zoom is semantic): zooming out trades cell detail for structural summaries (names over blocks, summaries over cells); text never shrinks below legibility, swapping level-of-detail instead.
why: Keeps large sheets and model maps legible at every zoom level.

statement: Inherited Strand spine laws: calc-state/focus is the only saturated channel (amber), provenance is structural tint never decoration, and authoring is modeless 1-bit.
why: Carries forward three non-negotiable visual laws from SPINE.md.

statement: Strand chrome and paper palette tokens: `petrol-800` (#193F49) for Mast/Bridge/Strip/instrument chrome, `petrol-900/950` (#12303A / #0C1C22) for chrome depth ramp and dark chrome, `charcoal` (#353938) for dark-theme paper base and body ink, and `mist` (#EDF1F2) for light paper base and chrome ink.
why: Defines the exact ground and chrome colors of the Strand flight-deck surface.

statement: Strand structural and identity palette tokens: `teal-600` (#318995) for structure, references, interactive accents, and Excel-strict identity; `teal-400` (#3DB6CF) for links, secondary structure, and OneCalc identity; `sage-400`/`forest-700` (#71A08A / #235949) for soft value tints (and legacy Rich-Tree identity pair).
why: Assigns consistent hues to structural links and product identity.

statement: Strand semantic signal tokens: `amber` (#FFB301) is the sole saturated focus/attention channel (cursor, selection, running calc, X-Ray target); `green-500` (#3F8B76) is fresh/verified values; `signal` (#FF8001) is external/volatile only (RTD, links, add-in-fed cells); `red` (#D02A23) is errors only—never emphasis or branding.
why: Guarantees each semantic color has one unambiguous meaning across the entire product.

statement: Strand identity and neutral rules: profile identity uses a two-block base-pair badge (distinct block-length pattern + color pair: OneCalc `dot-long`, Excel-strict `twin`, legacy Rich Tree `long-dot`) appearing only in chrome identity spots (profile badge, stage underline) and never on data surfaces; neutrals are petrol-biased greys derived from petrol/mist, never pure grey.
why: Ensures product/mode recognition survives small sizes and color-vision differences without polluting data surfaces.

statement: Accessibility doctrine: every color signal must pair with a non-color cue (shape, weight, or badge) so color is never the sole indicator.
why: Ensures full legibility for color-vision-deficient and high-contrast users.

statement: Strand Contrast Law (§2.1): surface tones are never used directly as text or small glyphs; per-theme `-ink` variants (`teal-ink`, `green-ink`, `ink-3`, `prov-const`, `prov-ext`, `red-ink` — including dark-paper red `#E4625C` because raw red fails AA on dark paper) must meet WCAG AA thresholds (>=4.5:1 for text/small glyphs and chrome ink on petrol; >=3:1 for large text, borders, and non-text marks), with scoped inks on dark chrome.
why: Prevents contrast regressions like dark ink bleeding onto petrol chrome or red errors failing on dark paper.

statement: Every sanctioned foreground/background token pair is enforced mechanically by `SANCTIONED_PAIRS` unit tests in `apps/dna-strand` (with derivations documented in `theme.rs`); on divergence between `STRAND.md` and the crate, the crate wins and the doc is updated, and any palette change breaking WCAG contrast fails the build.
why: Makes contrast compliance an automated invariant rather than a manual review step.

statement: Strand Type System (§3): UI & data use Recursive (sans-linear) with tabular figures (`tnum`); formulas & addresses use Recursive Mono (same skeleton, casual axis reserved for ghost text/hints); Notebook prose uses Source Serif 4 (~68ch measure, wider leading, annotation layer only); Windows-first fallback chain (Segoe UI Variable/system-ui, Cascadia Code/Consolas, Charter/Georgia); single modular scale (11, 12.5, 13.5, 15.5, 18, 22, 27), weights 480/560/650, +0.12em uppercase tracking, and `text-wrap: balance` on headings.
why: Unifies numeric, formula, UI, and prose typography while keeping tabular alignment crisp.

statement: Strand Block Geometry (§4): corner radii track block size (chips/tokens 5px, grid cells 0px, cards 9px, panels and stage corners 14px); gap scale is 2, 4, 6, 10, 14, 22px; formula tokens, name chips, node cards, and map districts share one component family, border treatment, and hover/focus grammar (amber outline, 1px offset).
why: Keeps component proportions and focus cues uniform across every view.

statement: Strand Motion & Density (§5): durations are 120-160 ms on a standard deceleration curve with `prefers-reduced-motion` honored everywhere; only three animations are sanctioned—state settle (focus/selection), recalc ripple (following real `evaluation_order`), and cross-stage continuity halo (mechanism 09); two density modes exist—Working (default, hands-density) and Reading (Notebook/published, looser leading and wider measure)—with no third mode.
why: Keeps motion informative and prevents uncontrolled density sprawl.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Strand Theming (§6): CSS custom properties use the `--dna-*` prefix with three themes (`cockpit-light` default, `cockpit-dark`, `high-contrast`) replacing the old 16-skin visual-theme concept; all tokens come from one `dna-strand` crate with no per-skin stylesheets beyond component-scoped rules resolving through tokens.
why: Centralises theme maintenance and guarantees every skin responds uniformly to theme switches.

statement: Strand Do/Don't rules (§7): keep all readouts in the Strip or Inspector (never scatter status into the stage); use provenance tints structurally (constants/formulas/external) and never color-code sheets or nodes decoratively; never introduce a new saturated color for a new feature (attention = amber, external = signal, broken = red); cut any animation carrying no state info; parity/evidence marks reuse standard semantic colors under a distinct twin-block glyph family (never a new hue, never amber); treat the design language as versioned, never 'final'.
why: Prevents gradual visual drift and hue inflation as features are added.

statement: Linked-boxes mapping over defined names: each box is a named calculation unit whose inputs and outputs map to dotted Excel defined names (e.g. `MyCell.Input1`, `MyCell.Result`); wiring `OtherCell.Output` to `MyCell.Input1` sets `MyCell.Input1` to `=OtherCell.Output` (unwiring restores a literal or empty); box outputs are formulas over inputs displayed inside the box with the box prefix stripped (`= Input1 * 2`).
why: Represents box-and-wire diagrams using native Excel defined names so workbooks open and calculate in Excel without extensions.

statement: Linked-boxes layout (box positions, sizes, colors) is presentation-only metadata stored in a custom XML skin part, never in the calculation model, so Excel safely ignores it.
why: Preserves complete Excel file compatibility for spatial canvas layouts.

statement: Engine fit for linked boxes: leverages first-class defined names in calc-doc and the engine (scopes, LET/LAMBDA bodies, name calculation from dc-hsa5) and Excel's native support for dots in defined names (`MyCell.Input1`) without needing escaping or engine extensions.
why: Confirms box-and-wire semantics require zero non-Excel calculation features.

statement: Formula-name presenter and interpreter (Skin IR layer): a bidirectional AST-level transform over `calc-fml`'s syntax tree (never raw text, so strings, ranges, and functions are untouched) that Presents qualified names in skin context (`MyCell.Input1 * 2` -> `Input1 * 2` inside `MyCell` while keeping `OtherCell.Output` qualified) and Interprets user-typed short names back to full defined names before engine evaluation; reusable by both Model map and Notebook.
why: Lets non-grid views show and accept concise local names while sending exact standard Excel formulas to the engine.

statement: Open design questions recorded for linked boxes: workbook vs sheet-scoped box names (`Sheet1!MyCell.Input1`), displaying array/spill inputs and outputs as mini-tables on boxes, cycle handling (refuse vs iterative calc), bidirectional grid interplay (`=MyCell.Result` and grid ranges as inputs), reverse-importing boxes from existing dotted names, and whether it appears in OneCalc as a small playground.
why: Captures the core edge cases a Model map specification must settle.

statement: Owner direction (2026-11-12) on linked boxes: boxes and edges are an alternate display and formula editor over the backing sheet drawn from names, precedents, and dependents; dragging an edge rewrites formulas on the sheet, which stays the source of truth so the workbook opens unchanged in Excel.
why: Resolves reverse-import as the normal mode of operation and keeps the sheet authoritative.

statement: Owner direction (2026-11-12): views use only what Excel also exposes (names, formulas, precedents/dependents, pre/post-calc values, RTD, data tables, iterative-calc settings) so the same view can run as an Excel add-in; calculation events may drive visuals but never alter values.
why: Enforces the strongest possible Excel-compatibility boundary on view capabilities.

statement: Owner direction (2026-11-12): cycles are allowed where Excel allows them under iterative calculation (initially sketched as feedback through a delay; later refined in Pro 20/DECISIONS_20261126 to distinguish solved iterative loops from RTD-clock/macro-ticked delays); Ptolemy II-inspired directors operate strictly over plain Excel mechanisms (RTD events, iterative ticks, IFS mode cells, data-table sweeps), previewed in `names-in-motion.html` and `watershed.html` and tested by `dc-hul4`.
why: Grounds dynamical systems modelling and simulation directors entirely in plain Excel primitives.

statement: Pro 19 visual and conceptual baseline: base visual design on `STRAND.md` v0.1 (refinements allowed if explicitly justified), build on `LINKED_BOXES_SKIN.md`, and treat `names-in-motion.html` and `watershed.html` as static sketches to react to rather than specifications.
why: Aligns all multi-model design proposals to one shared visual language while permitting justified refinements.

statement: DNA Calc product baseline: exact Excel calculation (oddities included) and file round-trip compatibility across formulas, dynamic arrays, tables, names, charts, shapes, form controls, conditional formatting, macros, and add-ins; runs on desktop and browser with keyboard and mouse first (touch/pen noted where relevant, not designed now); six existing experimental views are rough sketches, not design constraints.
why: Defines the real capability footprint and input-device priority the UX must serve.

statement: Pro 19 settled direction recap: five persona views (Classic, Inspector, Notebook, Model map, App) with an optional read-only formula lens (names/LET/lambda); Formula Explorer tool inside workbooks (seeded from a cell's inputs) and standalone ('DNA Calc - Formula Explorer'); one shared shell with preferred/supported/per-sheet views stored in an Excel-preserved file part; declarative user/agent customisation; and 'No more than Excel' (model edits = Excel edits, presentation free, files must open in Excel).
why: Establishes the settled product constraints given identically to all Pro 19 design respondents.

statement: Shared cast fixture 1 — Budget: three sheets — Inputs (12 assumptions, 2 scenario columns), Monthly (12 periods across columns, revenue and cost blocks), and Summary.
why: Canonical multi-sheet financial planning model used across storyboards, mockups, and usability tests.

statement: Shared cast fixture 2 — Sales: a 25,000-row Orders table on one sheet used as a database, queried by a Report sheet via SUMIFS, XLOOKUP, and FILTER and summarised by a PivotTable.
why: Canonical sheet-as-database and reporting model for testing data frames, Inspector error tracing, and large tables.

statement: Shared cast fixture 3 — Loan: an inputs block, a 360-row amortisation schedule (PMT, IPMT, PPMT, running balance), and a chart.
why: Canonical consumer-facing model for App view, scenarios, printing, and agentic App generation.

statement: Shared cast fixture 4 — Stock: a small systems model of inventory with inflow, outflow, reorder delay, a deliberate circular reference solved by iteration, and a form-control slider for the reorder point.
why: Canonical systems-dynamics fixture for Model map feedback/delays, Inspector Live instruments, and iterative calc.

statement: Shared cast fixture 5 — Inherited: an Enron-class legacy workbook (~40 sheets including hidden sheets, ~300,000 formulas with one edge-to-edge packed sheet, missing external links, a VBA macro module, volatile OFFSET names, and unfixed errors).
why: Prevents toy-workbook design by forcing every view to handle messy enterprise reality honestly.

statement: Shared cast of six personas: Maria (finance analyst / Excel power user), Sam (reviewer/auditor), Lee (systems engineer), Jo (manager consuming models built by others), Ade (Excel add-in author), and an AI agent working alongside Maria.
why: Ensures every view and workflow is evaluated against concrete, distinct user goals.

statement: Seven mandatory end-to-end UX storyboards (convertible directly into usability-test scripts with success measures and cast screenshot coverage): (1) Maria opens Inherited and orients herself; (2) Maria turns Budget into a notebook write-up; (3) Sam traces a wrong number on Sales Report; (4) Lee builds Stock on Model map then checks Classic; (5) Jo runs Loan as an App, tries scenarios, and prints; (6) Ade loads an add-in in standalone Formula Explorer, tests a function, then uses it in Budget; (7) AI agent proposes a Budget change, Maria reviews, partially accepts, and undoes the rest.
why: Anchors the Design Book in concrete keystroke-and-click user journeys rather than abstract feature lists.

statement: Twelve make-or-break UX moments every workflow must specify: first run/empty states, feature discovery, loading/calculating feedback, view-switch continuity (what stays put vs moves), error/warning/refusal states, undo/recovery, cross-view and external copy/paste, hover/focus/selection feedback, perceived speed, accessibility (screen reader, keyboard-only, contrast, zoom), and Excel-user differences framed as clear wins rather than surprises.
why: Guarantees the Design Book resolves the micro-interactions that determine day-to-day usability.

statement: Required conceptual-model specification: universal target ontology (cell, range, block, name, table, object, view item), cross-view selection and navigation continuity, semantics of edits outside the grid, cross-view undo, visible errors/calc state/live data, and how agent actions are displayed, reviewed, accepted, and traced; plus per-view spec of gestures/keyboard, entry/exit, and cast-workbook suitability (including both docked and standalone Formula Explorer).
why: Ensures all five views and Formula Explorer obey one coherent interaction grammar.

statement: Baseline catalogue of 15 recurring real spreadsheet model patterns: sheet-as-database, inputs and assumptions, calculation blocks, time series with periods across, scenarios and sensitivity tables, reference tables, pipelines across sheets, running balances and deliberate circular references, simulations, control panels, pivots, live data, macro-driven models, reports and dashboards, and stocks/flows/feedback/delays.
why: Grounds view projections and pattern recognition in the real idioms found across business workbooks.

statement: Pattern recognition rubric: prefer what the program can infer from the file over mandatory user declaration, always allow user or agent confirmation/correction, and specify for each pattern how a person recognises it, how the program detects it and with what confidence, how it is confirmed/corrected, and how each view presents it.
why: Delivers useful structure automatically on legacy workbooks without silent misinterpretation.

statement: Big and busy workbook policy (evaluated on Inherited): each view must define when it shows everything, when it simplifies (blocks instead of cells, formula runs collapsed as one item, levels of detail, expand on demand, sampling with a visible notice), and when it declines with a plain explanation and way forward; set explicit opening, first-paint, and keystroke latency budgets; hangs, silently dropped content, and pictures misstating the model are never acceptable.
why: Guarantees honest graceful degradation on 300k-formula workbooks.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Customisation specification must define what a skin manifest declares, how a person or agent creates, tests, and shares one, and what remains fixed, validated by two worked examples: an agent restyling Classic and an agent building an App view of Loan from a three-line brief.
why: Tests the skin API against concrete end-to-end human and agent customisation tasks.

statement: Printing and macro automation specification: define exactly what each view prints and what a VBA macro can do to views (switch view, select target/block, show a panel).
why: Ensures print output and programmatic view control are designed coherently across all five views.

statement: Appendix A Classic keyboard and mouse conformance list must specify expected behaviour for key tips, navigation, F2, F4, F9, Ctrl+Enter, fill handle and double-click fill, drag-move and drag-copy, range-picking while typing a formula, and remaining Excel gestures.
why: Turns 'Excel-familiar' into a testable, auditable checklist.

statement: Design specifications must supply testable front-end requirements (R-1...), plain-language system needs (C-1... stating what the UI needs without dictating implementation), explicit push-back section for challenging settled assumptions, and risks/open owner questions/milestone order (no dates).
why: Creates a direct, traceable handoff from UX design into the skin-architecture plan.

statement: Mockup realism rule: use the cast workbooks' real labels, numbers, formulas, and errors (never placeholder text), show active/critical states (mid-edit, mid-calculation, error showing) rather than only resting screens, and ensure storyboards can run directly as usability tests and clickable prototypes.
why: Exposes layout overflow, density issues, and state-signalling flaws early.

statement: Pro 19 anti-patterns and IP constraints: never use Microsoft icons, fonts, ribbon artwork, or styling (familiar structure, own visual design); avoid copying Excel's look, inventing calculation features Excel lacks, proliferating confusing modes, hiding the grid from grid users, abstract unbuildable mockups, generic UX platitudes, or feature lists without flows.
why: Establishes hard legal, architectural, and usability guardrails.

statement: Pro 20 Strand refinement adopted: amber inner accent paired with a dark outer focus stroke, plus explicit visual state distinctions across cell and UI states, targeting the craft/density/liveliness bar of `names-in-motion.html` and `watershed.html` without their execution-semantics shortcuts.
why: Solves amber focus contrast on light paper while raising visual craft to shipped-product fidelity.

statement: Owner-accepted Pro 19 core commitments (reaffirmed in Pro 20): one workbook/selection/undo history; every non-grid edit labelled model vs presentation change before commit; agent proposals as reviewable units applied together with separate undo steps and stale-proposal conflicts; all five push-backs accepted (circular ref != delay, dependency != execution recording, lens never rewrites formula, tested save routes for view settings, intact file != runs everywhere); milestone order accepted.
why: Locks down the foundational interaction and honesty contracts entering full-fidelity mockups.

statement: Pro 20 refinement on calculation order: an observed calculation order may appear as an optional Inspector detail, strictly labelled 'DNA Calc's calculation order' and never presented as Excel's calculation order.
why: Provides useful diagnostic visibility while staying truthful about engine-specific evaluation order.

statement: Pro 20 Change 1 — Quiet surface with honesty underneath: state indicators appear only when abnormal (pending, stale, previous, error, missing source, or calculating longer than a moment); a clean current workbook displays no status text, only a small steady mark; revision numbers appear in History and print footers rather than on working screens.
why: Eliminates visual noise on healthy workbooks without sacrificing any diagnostic honesty when anomalies arise.

statement: Pro 20 Change 2 — App inputs recalculate results live by default (typing a valid value updates immediately and Undo reverses it); 'Apply inputs' batching is an explicit option for slow models or author choice, with the reason visibly stated.
why: Matches spreadsheet immediacy by default while gracefully supporting heavy/slow models.

statement: Pro 20 Change 3 — Inspector Live panel (Phyphox spirit): plots RTD feeds, volatile functions, and chosen cells as live signals over time with Record, Pause, and Clear controls; displays min, max, last value, update rate, and honest coalescing readouts; supports replaying a recorded run against the dependency explanation (demonstrated on Stock slider + Sales RTD price feed).
why: Realises the Phyphox live-instrument vision for dynamic and RTD-driven spreadsheets.

statement: Pro 20 Change 4 — Full Notebook components: dynamic arrays and Tables presented as typed data frames (column types, summary row, row window over 25,000 orders, sort/filter explicitly labelled 'view only' vs 'changes the Table'), inline cell-bound controls (slider, dropdown, checkbox), live-updating inline charts, live RTD values embedded in prose, and a horizontal cross-sheet pipeline layout (Inputs > Monthly > Summary).
why: Demonstrates rich analytical notebook blocks backed by ordinary Excel structures.

statement: Pro 20 Change 5 — Alive Model map: hierarchy drill-down with breadcrumbs, ports showing live values, a source toggle, a parameter rail, click-to-inspect, and value motion along wires after an input changes strictly labelled 'dependency explanation'; Stock's reserve loop is drawn as an iteration enclosure while its three-day lag is drawn as a period-labelled delay.
why: Brings visual liveliness to Model map while preserving strict semantic distinction between iteration and delay.

statement: Pro 20 Change 7 — Ticked simulation via RTD clock: drive time-stepped models with an Excel-loadable RTD server such as `=RTD("DnaCalc.Clock",,"Stock","tick")` exposing run/pause, step, rate (ticks/sec), and reset-at (tick count or condition cell); each tick triggers one recalculation advancing self-referencing state cells by one iterative step, making the previous value a true per-tick delay (`z^-1`); Model map infers ticked vs solved cycles strictly from file evidence (clock RTD topic, iteration settings, self-reference pattern) and labels ambiguous cycles 'unknown'.
why: Provides genuine, Excel-compatible discrete-time simulation without conflating ordinary circular references with delays.

statement: Stock (ticked) cross-view presentation: Model map shows the RTD clock as a source block with controls, state cells as delays labelled 'per tick (RTD clock)', and the within-calculation reserve loop beside them as an iteration enclosure; Inspector Live panel plots stock-on-hand per tick with pause/step/reset; App view exposes run, pause, step, and a rate slider for Jo.
why: Proves ticked simulation works consistently across modeller, auditor, and consumer views.

statement: Pro 20 Change 6 — Visible Classic keyboard and mouse states: explicitly design and verify Alt key-tip overlays on command bands, formula range-picking with colored reference outlines, F4 anchor cycling, fill-handle mid-drag preview, Ctrl+Enter multi-cell fill, drag-move, Alt+Q command search with results, and clearly distinct focus, selection, hover, and edit states.
why: Makes Classic interaction states visually crisp and testable rather than implied.

statement: Full-fidelity design-system and mockup verification bar (Pro 20): 1440x900 desktop framing plus 200% zoom, high-contrast, and reduced-motion variants; complete Strand component sheet (tokens, type scale, 10 cell states: normal/selected/active/editing/point-mode/error/spill-anchor/spill-child/stale/pending, chips/cards, shell chrome, 4 drawer types: model-change/presentation-change/agent-proposal/conflict, ports/wires, focus/hover/selection); self-contained offline HTML (no external requests or Microsoft styling); exact fixture arithmetic verified against formulas, real dense grids/SVG charts, side-mounted callouts, and keyboard-navigable steps.
why: Sets an objective visual and arithmetic fidelity standard for design artifacts and UI acceptance.

statement: Pro 21 Section A correction — Jupyter computation chain: the Notebook is first an always-visible chain of input formula -> result directly beneath -> next input building on that result -> its result, with Pluto/Excel live reactivity (no run button, no stale cells) and prose sitting between chain links; presentation layouts (reading view, horizontal pipeline) are secondary views of that same chain (note: separate read-mode presentation later dropped in DECISIONS_20261126 D-6).
why: Corrects earlier presentation-first framing so Notebook genuinely serves step-by-step live computation.

statement: Pro 21 A1 — Computation cells and typed outputs: an analyst writes formula cells such as `=FILTER(Orders, Orders[Status]="Pending")` yielding a typed data frame beneath, followed by `GROUPBY`/`PIVOTBY` and `SORTBY` building on it by name and a cell turning it into an inline chart, with full formula editing, completion, and signature help.
why: Shows modern Excel dynamic-array analytics operating naturally in a Jupyter-style notebook workflow.

statement: Pro 21 A2 — Named cell outputs and navigation: each notebook output can be given a name (e.g. `pending`, `byRegion`) referenced by downstream cells, with a clear UI to assign names and jump back from any reference to the defining cell.
why: Replaces cryptic A1 addresses with readable notebook variables backed by real workbook names.

statement: Pro 21 A3 — Reactive in-place editing: editing an upstream notebook cell (e.g. changing a filter or date criterion) immediately updates every downstream output, inline chart, and inline prose value in place, briefly marking recalculated cells with nothing left stale.
why: Delivers Pluto/Excel reactivity without Jupyter's out-of-order stale-cell failure mode.

statement: Pro 21 A4 — Function cells (`=LAMBDA(...)`): a notebook cell can define a reusable `=LAMBDA(...)` (e.g. margin % or aged bucket) stored as a workbook defined name, visually distinct from a value cell, and callable by cells below.
why: Gives notebook analysts first-class reusable helper functions within standard Excel semantics.

statement: Pro 21 A5 — Prose, controls, and RTD between computation cells: Markdown text cells embed live inline values, cell-bound control panels (dropdowns, sliders) drive downstream analysis, and live RTD feeds integrate directly into notebook computations.
why: Unifies narrative explanation, interactive parameters, and live data inside one computation chain.

statement: Pro 21 A6 — Visible Excel backing-sheet mapping for Notebook: every computing cell must map to a real cell or defined name in the workbook (e.g. a visible `Analysis` sheet holding formulas in reading order with spill headroom, workbook names for named outputs, and prose stored as presentation in the view part) so Excel computes identically; Classic can show each notebook cell's backing range outlined, and the layout must explicitly manage spill growth so growing arrays do not collide with the next cell's backing range.
why: Makes Notebook's relationship to the underlying Excel file transparent and spill-safe.

statement: Pro 21 A7 — Live tree extension: any formula cell can expand inline into a live tree of its LET bindings or nested arguments, displaying each node's current evaluated value directly under the cell (also available in Formula Explorer).
why: Makes complex LET/nested formulas inspectable in place without leaving the notebook.

statement: Pro 21 A8 — Exploration to report without copying: switching a notebook analysis into a clean write-up presentation operates over the exact same backing cells rather than making a copy (note: DECISIONS_20261126 D-6 later routes reader-style presentation to the App / easy forms maker view rather than a separate Notebook read mode).
why: Avoids stale copy-paste reports by keeping presentation bound to live calculation cells.

statement: Pro 21 B1 — Recognised pattern workflow: expose workbook pattern recognition with four provenance states ('From workbook', 'Suggested', 'Confirmed by Maria', 'Needs review after change'), supporting a workbook-level overview of Inherited, a 'Why suggested' confirm/correct flow (e.g. Budget's Monthly time series), and recognising Sales' Orders Table as a database queried by Report.
why: Makes inferred workbook structure inspectable, editable, and resilient to subsequent workbook edits.

statement: Pro 21 B2 — Mixed views per sheet and file view settings UI: sheet tabs visibly indicate their per-sheet view (e.g. notebook, grid, map in one workbook), and a file view-settings UI lets authors set preferred and supported views, inspect what is stored in CustomXML, and see what a reader without DNA Calc layout sees.
why: Makes mixed-view workbooks and Excel fallback transparent to authors and recipients.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Pro 21 B3 — Customisation studio: provides 'Edit this layout' showing the declarative manifest beside a live preview, theme token editing with live Strand contrast checks, a keymap editor highlighting any binding that departs from the Classic conformance profile, and agent-authored customisation review (dark theme variant judged against Strand; Loan App built from a three-line brief with reviewable binding proposal).
why: Makes declarative skin authoring and agent customisation transparent, contrast-safe, and keymap-safe.

statement: Pro 21 B4 — Shell File and Print flows: File screen supports Open, Recent, Templates, and New from a model pattern (e.g. 'inputs, monthly model, summary'); Save shows a quiet notice that view settings travel in the file; Print preview covers Notebook and Model map regions alongside App print proof.
why: Completes the shared shell lifecycle across all persona views.

statement: Pro 21 B5 — Model map at scale: shows Inherited at sheet-group level with counted inter-group relationships, displays a plain refusal message when 'expand all cells' is requested, allows drilling into one sheet group's blocks, and supports an optional sheet page inside the map.
why: Proves Model map scales gracefully to 40-sheet / 300k-formula workbooks.

statement: Pro 21 B6 — Macro security levels renamed to Off / Guarded / Unguarded (replacing 'Safe' with 'Guarded'); UI must cover an App button running a VBA macro under Guarded mode with a trust notice, a macro switching views and selecting a block via the views library, and a plain refusal readout when a macro attempts a blocked action.
why: Avoids over-promising absolute safety with the word 'Safe' while making macro trust and refusals explicit.

statement: Pro 21 B7a — Standalone Formula Explorer function browser: organises the catalogue by family with search, signature, argument help, and examples, displaying each function's real DNA Calc Excel-match status (e.g. '4,252 / 4,311 calls match Excel; worst 63 ulp') and a plain refusal reason for unimplemented functions.
why: Turns DNA Calc's oracle test evidence into a transparent, user-facing trust feature.

statement: Pro 21 B7b — Standalone Formula Explorer formatting playground: applies number formats, locales, and conditional-format rules to a spilled array result while keeping raw underlying values and formatted display text visibly apart.
why: Lets users test locale/format/CF edge cases without creating a workbook and prevents format-vs-value confusion.

statement: Pro 21 B7c — Standalone Formula Explorer add-in library view: lists loaded `.xll` and `.xlam` add-ins with their functions, categories, argument descriptions, and explicit indicators of what the level-0 host can and cannot run.
why: Gives add-in developers an honest, workbook-free testbench for UDFs.

statement: Pro 21 B8 & verification rigor: interactive mockups and UI states must keep all derived readouts strictly synchronised with simulation state (e.g. tick breadcrumb and captured-state counter advancing with every tick), and every shown computing-cell output (including `GROUPBY`/`PIVOTBY` aggregates over the 25,000-row Sales fixture) must be arithmetically verified and documented in `verification.html`.
why: Catches subtle UI state-sync bugs and prevents fabricated numbers in design verification.

statement: DECISIONS_20261126 overriding authority & coherence rule: these owner and decider rulings override any disagreeing source; the Design Book must tighten the UX into one coherent design to tell DNA Calc's stories—avoiding a mess of vaguely overlapping ideas—and place every rejected idea in Appendix Z with an explicit reason.
why: Prevents design-by-committee sprawl while maintaining a lossless audit trail.

statement: DECISIONS_20261126 website & app synergy: while the UI makes the first impression, automation, engine use, cross-platform support, and agentic tweaking must also be foregrounded on the website, and the DNA Calc app and website must connect with links both ways and share the same stories.
why: Connects product discovery, documentation, and in-app experience into one cohesive narrative.

statement: Owner Ruling 1 (Merge method): execute ledger-first merge as specified in `MERGE_PROMPT_PROVISIONAL.md`—Neon performs Stage 1 extraction, while Fable and Opus perform clustering, decisions, and writing the Design Book.
why: Establishes clear accountability and prevents ideas from being dropped during synthesis.

statement: Owner Ruling 2 (Standalone Formula Explorer): ship standalone 'DNA Calc - Formula Explorer' early as a teaser.
why: Delivers an immediate, high-signal public taste of DNA Calc's Excel parity and formula UX before full workbook UI completion.

statement: Owner Ruling 3 (Ticked models): the RTD clock is right for DNA Calc's example ticked models, while ticking real Excel models from a macro engine (via value changes, volatile inputs, and Calculate calls) is also valid; RTD has advantages over macros plus events, but this is not set in stone.
why: Supports RTD-clock examples cleanly without excluding real-world macro-ticked Excel models.

statement: Owner Ruling 4 (Undo across a macro run): attempt it and design the architecture for it, acknowledging it is a deep non-trivial challenge, and do not promise it in the first release.
why: Preserves architectural headroom for macro undo without blocking v1 delivery.

statement: Owner Ruling 5 (Notes and findings): store notes and findings in a `customXml` part now; a visible-sheet mirror is optional and not necessarily always on; ship a working solution now and expect to improve it with experience.
why: Avoids polluting user sheets by default while leaving room for Excel-visible mirroring when wanted.

statement: Owner Ruling 6 (Notebook modes — overrides separate Author/Read mode proposals): Notebook works exactly like Jupyter; Read-only is purely a file-open mode (cannot be edited), with NO separate read-mode presentation inside Notebook—reader-style presentation belongs to the easy forms maker (App) view.
why: Eliminates the confusing Author vs Read mode split inside Notebook and clarifies App's distinct role.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Owner Ruling 7 (FerroUI): not at this stage; keep the WebView2/Leptos baseline and close `dc-etcxb.3` as not now.
why: Focuses engineering effort on the skin architecture and Design Book rather than a GUI toolkit rewrite.

statement: Owner Ruling 8 (Website tagline): drop 'spreadsheet for your workbooks'; the Design Book must propose a stronger hook.
why: Replaces a weak tagline with messaging that conveys DNA Calc's modern views over Excel compatibility.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Owner Ruling 9 (Skin architecture is central): Fable (thinking max) and Opus (thinking extra high) each design the skin architecture independently, then merge into one architecture to reshape the codebase so subsequent UI work is easy and beautiful.
why: Gets two independent deep architectural designs before committing the codebase structure.

topic: XII. Customisation and the skin API
statement: Owner Ruling 10 (Fresh UI implementation — overrides micro-step migration): after the Design Book, create beads and write the new UI code fresh against the clean skin interface, discarding large chunks of the current skin code rather than planning a micro-step migration; publish early for feedback and iterate.
why: Avoids dragging legacy skin debt through slow incremental rewrites once the clean skin interface exists.

statement: Decider Ruling 11 (Key tips): Classic view uses Excel's exact key-tip letters; bit-matching Excel applies to Classic's keyboard bindings as well.
why: Prevents broken muscle memory for Excel keyboard power users.

statement: Decider Ruling 12 (View-switching keys): `Ctrl+Alt+1..5` switch between the five views unless Excel already binds a combination (decider checks for collisions); command search serves as the fallback.
why: Gives fast direct view switching while guaranteeing zero collisions with Classic Excel shortcuts.

statement: Decider Ruling 13 (Hidden names as anchors — overrides FRONT_END_SCOPE & IB-0041): never add hidden defined names as anchors (per Fable's argument); store anchors in our `customXml` part, keyed to cells and the user's own defined names.
why: Keeps the user's Name Manager clean and prevents hidden-name side effects in Excel.

statement: Decider Ruling 14 (Agent change trail): persist the agent's change trail in the workbook inside the same `customXml` part as notes and findings, with an opt-out toggle and the same 'improve later' rule.
why: Preserves reviewable provenance for AI-assisted edits inside the workbook while allowing users to disable it.
